overview:
Around 550 BCE a minor king from Fars in southwestern Iran, Cyrus II, overthrew his Median overlord Astyages and took Ecbatana. Within fifteen years he had absorbed the Lydian kingdom of Croesus in Anatolia and, in October 539, walked into Babylon and its empire. His son Cambyses II added Egypt in 525. That was three of the ancient Near East's great powers folded into one state in a single generation — a stretch of territory running from the Aegean and the Nile to the Hindu Kush that was, by a wide margin, the largest political unit the world had yet seen. The dynasty's own founding story was written later and for a purpose: Darius I, who seized the throne in 522 amid a contested succession, carved into a cliff at Behistun the claim that the man he killed was an impostor magus named Gaumata and that he himself descended from an ancestor called Achaemenes. Historians have never fully believed either claim, and the name we give the whole empire comes from that piece of usurper's propaganda.

What held it together was administration rather than uniformity. Territory was parcelled into satrapies under governors answerable to the king, linked by royal roads with relay stations, a standardized gold coinage, and Aramaic as an imperial working language layered over the local ones. Conquered peoples generally kept their gods, laws, and temples — Cyrus authorized the return of exiled Judaeans to Jerusalem, a decision that lodged him in the Hebrew Bible as a divinely appointed liberator. Clay tablets excavated at Persepolis in the 1930s, the Fortification and Treasury archives, show the machinery from underneath: rations of grain and beer issued to work gangs and travelling officials between roughly 509 and 457 BCE, in Elamite, Aramaic, Akkadian, Greek, and other scripts, with women workers drawing pay alongside men and offerings made to Ahuramazda and to Elamite gods in the same ledgers.

The empire is best known in the West for the wars it lost at its western fringe — the Ionian Revolt from 499, Marathon, Xerxes' invasion of Greece and the reverses at Salamis and Plataea in 480–479 — episodes marginal to Persian concerns but central to the Greek writers through whom most narrative history of the empire survives. It remained formidable for another century and a half, and Artaxerxes III reconquered a long-rebellious Egypt in 343. Then Alexander of Macedon crossed the Hellespont in 334, broke the imperial armies at Issus and Gaugamela, burned Persepolis, and pursued Darius III until the king was murdered by his own men in 330. His killer Bessus declared himself Artaxerxes V and held out in Bactria until he too was taken and executed in 329, the point at which the dynasty finally runs out.
significance: The Achaemenids invented the template for large multi-ethnic empire that everything after them worked from: provincial governors under a central court, a road and courier network, tribute assessed by region, a common administrative language, and toleration of local cult and custom as a deliberate instrument of rule rather than an oversight. Alexander's successors, the Parthians and Sasanians, and arguably Rome all inherited pieces of it. Its cultural afterlife is just as long — Cyrus survives as a liberator in Jewish scripture, the Persepolis reliefs became a touchstone for later Iranian dynasties and for modern Iranian national identity, and the Greek accounts of the Persian Wars set up an enduring and much-abused rhetorical opposition between "East" and "West" that has shaped how Europeans narrated their own past ever since.
coverage: Written from general reference works and the record of the Persepolis archives; the dataset holds no events at all beneath this story, so nothing here can be shown on the map. The wider evidentiary problem is real: the connected narrative comes almost entirely from Greek writers hostile to Persia, above all Herodotus, while the Persian side survives as royal inscriptions that are proclamations rather than history, plus administrative tablets that are rich on rations and logistics and silent on politics and war — and only a fraction of the roughly 25,000-plus Persepolis tablets has been published. Reign dates, the truth of Darius's accession story, and the empire's actual internal workings are all still argued over.
